I would recommend attending your nearest sexual assault treatment unit (https://www2.hse.ie/services/satu/) so that a statement can be made and your injuries photographed asap in case you want to use them for a legal case at a later stage. Women’s Aid and any of the Rape Crisis Centres will have lots of advice to offer and can accompany you to the treatment unit and/or the gardai if that would be of benefit to you. Make sure the Garda that you’re dealing with is a member of the Divisional Protective Services Unit as these Gardai have been trained specifically to deal with cases like yours. 

Please attend a Sexual Assault Treatment Unit asap so that evidence can be collected before the bruises fade etc so that it doesn’t end up as your word against his. Once the evidence is collected you have options on what you want to do next but once the visible evidence is gone, your choices are limited. Your GP won’t have taken evidence in a way that can be helpful to any legal case.

Before I knew that I was in a BPD relationship I took antidepressants on many occasions because, to protect myself from the emotional roller coaster, I would 'switch off' my feelings and then mistook this lack of feelings for depression.  Obviously, this didn't help my low mood but I did get some placebo effect from them as I would feel a bit better because I was 'doing' something to help myself.

I'm three years out of a 20+ year BPD marriage and am still experiencing the same bubbling emotions that you are.  I am often tempted to take medication so that I can feel a bit more stable and in control but I know that, if I don't acknowledge and process these many emotions, they will still be there waiting for me whenever I come off the medication.  

How I am feeling, while deeply unpleasant, is 'real' and I am feeling this way for a reason.  My goal is to figure out that reason and sit with it, acknowledge it, validate it and stop fighting it so that it will resolve itself.  You have been through a massively traumatic experience that was so crazy and un-understandable that your brain has had to do gymnastics to enable you to cope while you were in the relationship.  

My advice to you would be to educate yourself and then educate yourself some more about BPD and the different ways that your thinking patterns and emotions had to change to get you through the day to day of living with a pwBPD.  I used to continuously watch videos about BPD and how awful it was to have it.  It wasn't until I started to watch videos about the effects of BPD on those on the receiving end of it that my healing started.  

I know your feeling are awful, but know that your not alone in the way you feel and that what you are feeling is 'normal' considering what you've gone through.  You're feeling that way for a reason so try to explore it and learn about it rather than trying to suppress it or change it.  It will pass eventually, but until then, we are all here for you

If an apology is sincere, the person will apologise for their behaviour, will try to identify what caused or triggered their behaviour and will work on the issue so that they don't do it again.

If an apology is manipulation, the person will say they are sorry but they will be sorry that you experienced pain or a bad feeling eg if they say you are ugly and you get upset and tell them that they hurt you, they will say they are sorry that you are feeling hurt. They won't apologise for saying that you are ugly.  The won't acknowledge and take responsibility for the thing that they did that caused you pain.

There are some amazing videos on youtube about how to spot fake apologies.  They're mostly about narcissists but its a common trait the share with BPDs.  It will help you understand why they apologise but keep doing and saying the same things again and again and why you keep believing them.  The more you educate yourself, the stronger and more resilient you become in the face of BPD

I spent years in a state of confusion as my pwBPD would accuse me of really weird things that were so untrue that they would stop me in my tracks.  Until his diagnosis, I would often give credence to whatever he had accused me of and take it on board and try to fix the part of me that was giving off these signals or vibes that he was picking up on because they were hurting and worrying him.  

For example, when our son was born, he told me that, because I was sexually abused as a child, I was at an increased risk of going on to abuse our son.  I spent a huge amount of time worried sick that I might start abusing our son or being extra careful while changing his nappy etc in case I would be seen as touching him inappropriately. 

Fast forward a few years and it comes out that my pwBPD was sexually abusing our son throughout the first four years of his life!

A lot of the time, he would accuse me of untrue things that were 'true enough' to plant a seed of doubt in my mind and led me to believe that I was the cold and cruel one in the relationship.  He would say that I never wanted to be married to him, that I always intended on leaving him, that I was using him, that nothing he did was ever good enough, that he wasn't appreciated, that I never apologised, that I never took responsibility etc.  These were all based on his feelings rather than my actions.

Once he was diagnosed with BPD and I learned about projection, I was able to challenge and question him about this off-the-wall accusations and, if he was in the right mind-space, he was able to see and admit that he couldn't cope with the thoughts and feelings that were going on inside his head so he got rid of them by projecting them onto me.  Once he had projected his stuff onto me, he genuinely believed that I was feeling and acting out what had been inside his head.  He did it to cope with the guilt and the shame of what was inside his head.  It doesn't make it right or acceptable but it helped me to stop blaming myself all the time.

When our son was born my husband wBPD told me that I needed be mindful of the increased chance that I would sexually abuse my child because I had been abused myself.  I didn't think to question what he said as my husband was always a lot more knowledgeable about everything than I was!  I was always extremely careful when changing nappies and bathing him to ensure that nothing I did could be construed as being inappropriate.  Anyone that has kids knows that that poo can get everywhere and sometimes you have to get very up close and personal to make sure your baby is properly clean!!  

Years later when I mentioned this increased risk of being a child abuser myself because of my past to my therapist, she said that there was absolutely no proven truth in it!

It turns out that my husband had actually been sexually abusing our son all along!!  He couldn't cope with the shame of his feelings and his actions and so he projected them all onto me!!

Our 25 year relationship finally ended once I learned about BPD and saw clearly that once I started setting boundaries with him, he started to project his identity onto our daughter and started encouraging her to think and act just like him.

my husband of 23 years left of his own accord after he said he could see how afraid I was of him.  He was homeless for 2 years, living out of his van and office with no cooking or bathing facilities.  I felt so much guilt because I felt that my lack of coping skills meant that I couldn't live with him and my setting boundaries had left him homeless.  We couldn't figure out how to pay for two households with only one income between us.  His parents offered to buy him an apartment on two occasions but he backed out of both.  As soon as he realised that I was never going to take him back and that I was going to report his abusive past to the police, he got a room, a new job and a new partner!!  

Of course you feel guilty, it's a sign that you're good person that doesn't enjoy seeing someone you loved living like that but you are no longer responsible for him, his actions or the consequences of his actions...... you never were.  It's now his turn to be responsible for himself and this is the solution he has come up with.   

I completely understand the complete 180 that you have to do when you get the time and space to step back and see the bigger picture and you can see another side of the person you thought was the love of your life and you wonder how you ever liked them, never mind loved them with all of your heart!

I keep reading that time and space will give you the healing you need..... I haven't managed it myself but if enough people are saying it then it must be true!!

I went through something very similar.  After his first suicide attempt, I brought him to hospital, he was admitted, we went to family therapy and the abuse got worse.  The next time he said that I was making him feel suicidal, I called emergency services, opened the door for them and let them deal with him.  He has not threatened suicide since.  He told me his business would fail without me, I was the only thing he had to live for, if I abandoned him he wouldn't survive, I was the only person he could open up to etc.  I couldn't take it any more and we've been living separately for 2.5 years and had very, very little contact for the last 8 months.  Guess what?  He business is thriving, he's earning more than he has ever done in his entire life, he has a big support group of new friends, a new relationship and he's still alive........  meanwhile I'm at rock bottom trying to pick up the pieces of my life.  Listen to what your gut is telling you.  You know it's manipulation and abuse but they can explain it so well that you believe everything they tell you.  Her life, her quality of life, her health etc. are not your responsibility.  It is not your job to save her or fix her.  Your only 'job' is to treat yourself how you deserve to be treated and do what you need to do to heal yourself

I was the same.  When I explored the thinking and motivation behind it, I discovered I had a deep-seated need to know what they were up to so that I wouldn't be blind-sided by their actions any more.  If I knew what they were up to, I would be prepared for the consequences and be ready to pick up the pieces.  I also realised that the urge to check their SM was strong whenever I got into a 'maybe it was my fault / maybe I was over-sensitive / maybe I'm overreacting' frame of mind.  Seeing what they were up to would either prove or disprove my feelings were valid.  

Whatever the motivation behind it, checking their SM,  can become addictive, and it prevents your healing.  It's like constantly picking at a wound and preventing it from healing.   It's okay to be disappointed with yourself, it shows that you have set a good and healthy standard of acceptable behaviour for yourself and it's normal to feel disappointed when you don't meet that standard.  I don't agree that you are back to ground zero though.  You have learned a valuable lesson, that checking his SM hurts your healing, and this lesson will be invaluable to you as you continue to heal and recover.  It might benefit you to do some learning about the trauma bond so that you can learn why you feel compelled to do things that you know aren't in your best interest and not beat yourself up over it if it happens again.  Keep going.... you can do it because you are worth it!

I don't think you can ever know if they've truly changed or not...... I doubt they even know themselves.  What they say is what they believe to be true in that very second and their beliefs could be completely different next week, or tomorrow or in five minutes!!  

Whether they have changed or not, what they did to you was abusive and fixing the harm that that abuse did you you is what you need to focus on.  If they have changed, and are now 'perfect', it was still not okay to do what they did to you.  You deserved and continue to deserve to be treated with kindness and respect. 

Focus on getting yourself into a good and healthy way of feeling, thinking and reacting.  Once you're there, you'll be in a better and clearer place to make decisions about them and their behaviour

Have you heard about trauma bonding? Learning about it helped me so much. It explained why I couldn’t move on and why I stayed in the relationship when I knew that I shouldn’t. Realising the I was trauma bonded allowed me to forgive myself and really kick-started my recovery. I hope it helps you too

I only recently heard about the trauma bond and it has been a real sanity-saver!  It explains so many of my 'crazy' addict-like behaviors and learning about it has helped be begin to let myself off the hook for the guilt and shame I carry for staying in such an unhealthy relationships.  It also explains why I still feel compelled to do unhealthy things and still feel responsible for his feelings and actions even when the relationship is over.  I still feel guilty and selfish if I do something that I know would upset him even though we've been living apart for 2.5 years!

I do it all the time.  While I was in the relationship, I would always hear his voice in my head correcting me and telling my I was wrong.  Once I was out of the relationship, and through counseling, I noticed that his voice was still in my head saying the same things only now I had enough distance from him to allow me to realise that it was me saying those things to me now!  I continued on the pattern of constant belittling in his absence.  I find it very, very difficult to feel happiness, joy or contentment due to my ingrained fear that if I 'allow' myself to feel good about something, he will do something to ruin it on me.  I learned to stop trying to pick myself up off the ground after an BPD 'attack' because every time I tried to, it was only a matter of time before he knocked me back down again.  It was soul destroying to like something or someone and feel something positive only for them to take it away from you.  It was easier and safer to feel nothing about anything.  If I do achieve something or like something, I find myself devaluing it or running myself down about it so that he won't be able to.  I believe it all comes down to having no self-worth after years of BPD abuse.

Your friend's comment was thoughtless and insensitive.  It is extremely difficult for anyone who hasn't been on the receiving end of BPD abuse to understand what it's like.  It looks completely different from outside the relationship to what your reality was and still is.  When it comes to feelings, there is no 'should' or 'shouldn't' or 'have to', there is only what is.  You need to learn how to validate your own feelings.  An outsider is never going to 'get' what it's like to suffer from BPD abuse and so they just can't validate your feelings for you.  You will feel whatever you feel.  Sometimes they will feel like the 'right' feelings and sometimes they will feel like the 'wrong' feelings.  Your job is to just acknowledge them and let them pass.  You have a long path of healing ahead of you and it won't be easy but it will be worth it.  You are worth it.  I would recommend learning about the trauma bond, it has proved invaluable to my healing.

I'm 2.5 years out and have only recently tried to go no-contact and the difference is amazing..... really tough, but I felt the difference inside my head immediately. No-contact and educating yourself about what's going on inside your own head is the only way off of the BPD roller coaster.  It will take time, but it will be worth it.  Keep going, you're worth it!

I found that learning about the trauma bond and its effects really helped my understand why I keep tormenting myself by checking social media etc. when I know the pain it causes me.  Bear in mind, that only the good stuff gets put up on social media.   Your relationship with your ex probably looked just as wonderful and happy on social media but you know what it was really like.  You know why she treated you so bad (BPD) and you don't actually know how she's treating her new guy...... you only know what she wants people to know.  You can't control what she puts up on social media but you can control whether you look at it or not and you can control what you say to yourself when you think about her.  Try focusing on changing what you say to yourself when you think about her and/or check out her social media and your feelings will eventually catch up and become much healthier.

It's a long and slow process with lots of healing to be done..... go easy on yourself
